title: HKMA Weighs Agentic AI For Real-Time Blockchain Surveillance And Fund Freezing
excerpt: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority is exploring agentic AI systems to monitor blockchain activity and banking transactions for freezing crypto funds, according to a development that positions the regulator at the frontier of automated financial surveillance. The initiative, which remains in an exploratory phase, signals Hong Kong's intent to deploy autonomous artificial intelligence capable of making enforcement decisions without direct human intervention at each step. The core announcement centers on the HKMA's interest in agentic AI—systems that can independently pursue goals, make decisions, and take actions rather than merely responding to prompts. Unlike conventional machine learning models that flag suspicious patterns for human review, agentic AI would theoretically identify, assess, and act on illicit blockchain activity in near real time. The HKMA has not disclosed a formal timeline, vendor selection, or pilot scope as of this report. HKMA Weighs Agentic AI For Real-Time Blockchain Surveillance And Fund Freezing. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority's exploration of agentic AI represents a significant escalation in the regulator's technological capabilities. The authority is examining whether autonomous AI systems can monitor both on-chain blockchain activity and traditional banking transactions simultaneously, creating a unified surveillance layer that spans the crypto-fiat boundary. The initiative matters because Hong Kong has positioned itself as a regulated hub for virtual asset service providers under its licensing regime that took effect in June 2023. The HKMA's interest in agentic AI suggests the regulator believes existing monitoring tools are insufficient for the scale and speed of modern crypto transactions. Blockchain networks process transactions continuously across jurisdictions, and freezing funds often requires action within minutes—not the days or weeks typical of traditional financial investigations. The current status remains exploratory. The HKMA has not issued a formal consultation paper, tender, or regulatory circular on agentic AI for fund freezing. The authority's public statements on AI have focused on its potential to enhance supervisory efficiency, but specific details about agentic AI deployment for enforcement actions remain undisclosed. The Regulatory Gap Agentic AI Would Fill. Hong Kong's current crypto oversight relies on licensed exchanges and custodians reporting suspicious transactions through conventional channels. The Securities and Futures Commission and the HKMA share responsibility for virtual asset oversight, but their monitoring capabilities depend largely on data provided by regulated entities themselves. Agentic AI would theoretically allow the HKMA to independently monitor public blockchain ledgers, identify wallet addresses associated with sanctioned entities or criminal activity, and initiate freezing orders through banking partners without waiting for exchange self-reporting. This represents a shift from reactive to proactive enforcement—a capability no major financial regulator has publicly demonstrated at scale. How Agentic AI Could Distinguish Legitimate Crypto Transactions From Illicit Ones. The technical mechanism behind agentic AI blockchain monitoring involves multiple layers of analysis. An agentic system would first ingest blockchain data—transaction hashes, wallet addresses, token flows, and smart contract interactions—then cross-reference this against banking transaction records, sanctions lists, and known criminal wallet clusters. The distinction between legitimate and illicit transactions presents the core technical challenge. Blockchain transactions are pseudonymous by design, and legitimate privacy tools like coin mixers and privacy coins can make illicit activity indistinguishable from lawful financial privacy. Banks Block Third-Party AI Agents From Accounts
excerpt: . Banks Block Third-Party AI Agents From Accounts. Royal Bank of Canada, TD Bank and BMO are restricting personal AI agents from accessing online banking, citing security concerns. Updated on Nov. 22, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence. Live Poll. Would you ever give an AI assistant your online banking login?. Royal Bank of Canada posted a customer notice on October 27, 2026, saying it has blocked third-party personal AI agents from direct access to its authenticated digital properties, including online banking. TD Bank and BMO have introduced similar measures, while customers can still use official bank websites, mobile apps and customer service. Why it matters. AI agents are apps that take actions on a user's behalf, and many require a username and password to reach a bank account, which the banks say exposes confidential information. For Canadian customers, the restrictions mean that automated tools may no longer be able to manage banking tasks directly, though the banks say the measures are a security step rather than a problem with customer accounts. RBC's connections for third-party AI agents will stop working, while customers can still reach their accounts through the official website, mobile app and customer service. The source does not report how many customers use third-party AI agents or how many have been affected. The players. Royal Bank of Canada. Canada's largest bank by market capitalization, offering personal and commercial banking, wealth management and capital markets services across the country. TD Bank. A major Canadian bank headquartered in Toronto with large retail banking operations in Canada and the United States. BMO. The Bank of Montreal, one of Canada's oldest and largest banks, providing personal, commercial and wealth management services. Meta. The parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, which developed the Muse AI agent. The details. Meta's Muse, launched in September, is an AI agent that can open a browser, fill out forms and negotiate on users' behalf, and Meta said credentials shared with it are placed in secure storage. RBC's Digital Banking Security Guarantee states the bank will not reimburse losses if customers share passwords or Personal Verification Questions, and its guarantee covers transactions after customers report that their passwords may have become known to someone. Timeline. September 2026: Meta launches Muse and announces its credential storage approach. October 27, 2026: RBC posts its customer notice blocking third-party AI agents. November 4, 2026: TD publishes its article on restricting AI agent access to banking information. Related coverage. Personal Finance. Nov. 16. RBC Poll Finds AI Makes Holiday Scams Harder to Spot. Cybersecurity. Nov. 19. KPMG Canada Reports Client Tax Documents Accessed. Jobs. Nov. 19. TD Launches $2 Billion North American Initiative. The Tech Race. The restrictions show Canadian banks drawing a line against agents such as Meta's Muse, which operate by logging in with user credentials and acting in browsers on a customer's behalf. The move sets banks apart from the broader push by technology firms to make AI agents act across more online services. Customers who rely on third-party AI agents to manage banking will need to use the RBC, TD or BMO official website, mobile app or customer service instead. RBC's guarantee does not reimburse losses from shared passwords, so customers should be cautious about giving login details to any outside tool. The takeaway. Keep login details private and use official bank channels for account tasks, since the banks say credentials shared with AI agents can expose confidential information. Check your bank's security notices regularly, as policies on AI agent access are still changing. Further reading. For more on how these tools are reshaping online services, see Artificial Intelligence coverage. Source note: This article includes information reported by Bramptonist. Live Poll. title: Singapore Central Bank Tells Users Not to Give AI Agents Bank Logins; Know Your Agent Has No Date
excerpt: By Mark Rutherford Published: Nov 20 2026, 3:00 AM EST. Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Share on Reddit Share on Flipboard Share on WhatsApp. Singapore's central bank advised consumers on Thursday, Nov. 19, not to give personal AI agents the login credentials to their financial accounts and said it will help industry build a protocol that lets banks verify which agent is acting, for whom and with what authority. Chia Der Jiun, managing director of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), described the Know Your Agent (KYA) plan in a keynote at the Singapore FinTech Festival, where MAS also said it will rename its wholesale central bank digital currency (CBDC) test network the SG Digital Ledger and released an industry framework for tokenized collateral. Anyone who has pasted a banking password into an AI assistant is the audience here: MAS says there is not enough assurance of safety to recommend it, and what it offers in place of a login is a plan, not a product. Nothing announced Thursday is a finalized standard or certification, and MAS gave no delivery date for the KYA protocol. Banks May Not Know Whether Agent Acts Within Customer's Mandate. Chia said a bank receiving instructions from an agent may not know whether the agent has the customer's full authorization, whether it is staying inside its mandate, or who is responsible if it transacts incorrectly or beyond its instructions. He said some users already give agents their login credentials, and he cited insufficient assurance of safety in advising against it : "I would not advise giving personal agents such access. ". The same gap is visible in the United States. Axios reported on Oct. 22 that Morgan Stanley has blocked third-party agents from its platforms, and that JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Citi are restricting them, with agents mostly getting in through shared credentials that customers voluntarily share. Reuters said banks have been flagging and blocking transactions involving shared credentials, and many institutions are moving toward read-only access that lets agents retrieve information without executing transactions. A Morgan Stanley spokesperson told Axios the bank had not observed rogue AI agents accessing its platforms. Responsibility remains unassigned on both sides of the Pacific. Chia posed the liability question in his speech and did not answer it. Ted Miracco, CEO of the security firm Approov, argues that blame lies with customers who share credentials and with vendors that build agents to request them, yet neither clearly bears the financial consequences today. The reported incidents do not establish widespread theft or confirmed losses. KYA Protocol Would Exchange Agent Identity, Mandate and Provenance. MAS describes KYA as a "trusted information exchange" between customer agents and financial institutions. It would carry three kinds of facts : who the agent is and whom it represents, what authority and mandate it holds, and what assurance exists about its provenance and reliability. With that information, an institution could set terms and scope for each agent and open a dedicated, secure channel for it, which replaces borrowing the customer's own password. The difference matters technically. A login proves only that someone knows a password; it says nothing about what the holder was authorized to do. A scoped channel can bind each instruction to a stated mandate, which is the check banks cannot run on shared-credential sessions today. KYA builds on the first phase of MAS's Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime (SAFR) white paper, published July 3. SAFR places governance checkpoints that verify and record an agent's proposed actions before it executes them. Chia listed four lessons from that phase: autonomy needs defined boundaries, an agent's identity and authority must be clearly established, mandates must spell out permitted actions, limits and conditions, and controls must scale with the authority granted. title: Inter-American Development Bank Report Draws on AmericasBarometer Data to Examine AI Adoption in Latin America
excerpt: New Research. Inter-American Development Bank Report Draws on AmericasBarometer Data to Examine AI Adoption in Latin America. Read the Report. November 18, 2026 • AmericasBarometer. Share. The Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) has published From Digitalization to Artificial Intelligence: Turning Promises into Productivity , a new report examining how digital technologies and artificial intelligence can help accelerate economic growth, improve public services, and increase productivity across Latin America and the Caribbean. The report draws extensively on data from a special module on digital access, technology use, digital skills, and generative AI adoption included in the 2025–2026 AmericasBarometer, conducted by Vanderbilt University's LAPOP Lab. Implemented in 16 Latin American countries, the survey provides nationally representative data that form a central part of the report's analysis of digital adoption across the region. Among its findings, the report shows that 35% of adults in Latin America and the Caribbean report using generative AI in the previous three months, compared with 58% in the United States. AI adoption varies considerably across countries, with Argentina, Chile, and Uruguay reporting some of the region's highest rates. The findings also highlight persistent gaps in digital skills, access to government services online, and the integration of emerging technologies into everyday activities. The AmericasBarometer data serve as the primary empirical foundation for Chapter 3, Digital Adoption: Broad Access, Shallow Use , and inform analyses throughout the report. LAPOP Lab's María Fernanda Boidi, Director of Fieldwork and Regional Partnerships, and the LAPOP Lab team collaborated with the IDB to implement the survey module and deliver the data. The report underscores the importance of reliable, comparative public opinion data for understanding how technological change is unfolding across Latin America and the Caribbean and informing policies that promote inclusive digital transformation. title: McKinsey: Most AI users want advice from their bank’s AI, not Claude or ChatGPT
McKinsey Warns AI Agent Spending Could Undermine Banks' Automation Profits
excerpt: . Key takeaways. AI agent token spending could reach 20% of payroll. Human oversight adds substantial costs to banking automation. Autonomous financial assistants threaten traditional bank profit margins. Banks worldwide are facing an unexpected financial challenge as artificial intelligence agents become more expensive to operate, potentially consuming the savings institutions expect from automating customer service, compliance and administrative work. Ad. McKinsey warns that spending on AI tokens, the units used to process information through language models, could reach 20% of banks' total labor costs. The warning comes as global banking profits reached a record $1. 3 trillion in 2025, according to the firm's newly released Global Banking Annual Review. AI Agent Costs Could Reach 20% of Bank Labor Spending. Banks initially adopted AI assistants to accelerate routine work, including answering customer questions, reviewing documents and assisting compliance teams. Ad. However, autonomous agents create a different cost structure because they can execute multistep workflows, repeatedly query language models and communicate with other agents. McKinsey senior partner Vik Sohoni explained that conventional cost controls become less effective when agents interact continuously, allowing token consumption to accumulate rapidly. Some institutions have established AI FinOps teams to monitor computing expenses and direct workloads toward more economical models. Yet token spending represents only part of the problem. McKinsey's earlier research found that human oversight accounts for approximately 70%–75% of variable costs in certain banking customer-service workflows, compared with 20%–25% for tokens. That helps explain why banking AI regulation increasingly emphasizes human accountability and transaction-level controls. Banks Face Automation Savings That May Never Reach Profits. The economics become more complicated when employee productivity improves without reducing actual operating expenses. McKinsey's research found that AI agents reduced task completion times by approximately 60% across seven production systems at financial and professional services firms. Ad. However, shorter tasks do not automatically translate into smaller teams or lower payroll expenses. This distinction has become increasingly important as banks pursue workforce restructuring alongside technology investments. A bank might save two hours per employee through automation while continuing to pay the same salaries, plus additional AI subscription, infrastructure and supervision costs. AI Agents Could Also Threaten Banking Revenue. The financial risk extends beyond operating costs. McKinsey surveyed approximately 46,000 retail banking customers and found that 23% already use generative AI for financial tasks. Among customers using AI, 72% expressed willingness to delegate at least one financial task to an agent, although authorization limits remain a significant concern. This shift could accelerate autonomous financial transactions , allowing customers to compare savings rates and move deposits toward higher-paying institutions. For banks, that threatens a traditional source of revenue: inexpensive customer deposits used to fund interest-earning loans and investments. The development also introduces new payment liability risks , particularly when software executes transactions without individual human approval. Meanwhile, increasingly capable AI investment agents could expand automated financial decision-making beyond ordinary banking. News / Technology. title: Podcast: KI im Banking – Agenten übernehmen komplexe Prozesse
excerpt: KPMG. Klassische Assistenten wie ChatGPT oder Copilots gehören mittlerweile zum Büroalltag. Doch im Bankensektor kündigt sich bereits die nächste Evolutionsstufe an: Spezialisierte KI-Agenten, die als autonome Akteure komplexe Geschäftsprozesse übernehmen. Wie dramatisch der Effizienzsprung in der Praxis ausfällt, darüber diskutieren Chefreporter Jürgen Hill und Transformationsexperte Felix Flohr , Senior Manager im Bereich Financial Services bei KPMG, in der aktuellen Folge des Podcasts TechTalk – Voice of Digital. Hören Sie zudem, welche harten Regeln die Regulierung diktiert und wie Finanzinstitute mit klaren Sicherheitsarchitekturen Haftungsfallen und Kontrollverlust vermeiden können. So dauerte etwa das Auslesen von Handelsregistern und das Identifizieren komplexer Eigentümerstrukturen oft rund neun Stunden pro Fall. Das sichere die Datenqualität und verhindere gefährliche Single Points of Failure. title: Financial Supervisory Service Deploys AI to Accelerate Illegal Loan Reviews
excerpt: By Yu Jun-ho. Published 2026. 11. 22. 12:00 Updated 2026. 11. 22. 12:20. Financial authorities have introduced artificial intelligence (AI) to verify the invalidity of illegal high-interest loan contracts. The AI analyzes loan agreements and deposit records submitted by victims of illegal lending to assist in the review process. The speed of verifying evidence has increased by over 10 times compared to previous methods, accelerating relief for victims. According to the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) on the 23rd, the agency recently adopted an AI-based review system to determine the invalidity of illegal loan contracts. The review targets lending contracts with annual interest rates exceeding 60%. Such contracts legally exempt borrowers from obligations to repay both principal and interest. Victims can apply to the FSS to receive an "invalidity confirmation certificate" verifying this status. The certificate can be used to demand illegal lenders stop debt collection or as evidence in legal disputes. On September 29, a court acquitted a defendant in a criminal trial for the first time, citing an invalidity confirmation certificate issued by the FSS. Applications for the certificate have since surged. The challenge lies in the lengthy review process. Illegal lenders often fail to properly draft loan agreements, instead setting or altering terms via messenger conversations such as KakaoTalk. Each application typically includes dozens of evidentiary documents. Previously, FSS officers had to manually cross-check chat logs, promissory notes, and bank transfer records to calculate actual interest rates. Going forward, AI will analyze these materials to confirm loan terms, actual deposit amounts, and interest rates. According to the FSS, AI-based verification is over 10 times faster than manual processing. However, AI does not make final decisions on contract invalidity. Officers retain authority to approve certificate issuance as before. All data, including personal and financial information, is processed solely on the FSS’s internal AI servers to prevent external leaks. To obtain an invalidity confirmation certificate, victims must preserve chat logs with lenders and bank transfer records. Conversations detailing loan terms must be saved with visible dates, and bank statements verifying actual deposits and repayments must be submitted. Even if evidence is insufficient, applicants can follow FSS guidance to supplement it.
